content: When determining whether to implement a specific intervention, it is essential to compare it with other available options. These comparisons are often made using the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER), which evaluates the cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) or quality-adjusted life year (QALY) averted. For instance, a single HIV test during pregnancy has been demonstrated to be cost-effective across all epidemic settings. This is because it benefits the mother, prevents pediatric HIV infections, and reduces the lifetime treatment costs that would otherwise be required for an infected infant. However, retesting during late pregnancy is only cost-effective in settings with a high burden of HIV. In southern Africa, cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that additional testing strategies, such as HIV self-testing (HIVST), are more likely to be cost-effective when targeted at specific groups, such as men. Strategic planning for effective and efficient HIV testing services (HTS) requires understanding what can be implemented and scaled up within a given budget. Budget impact analysis (BIA) evaluates whether an intervention, even if cost-effective, is affordable within the available resources. This analysis helps guide decisions on resource allocation for new or existing HTS approaches. For example, in South Africa, a BIA of the optimal mix of HIV interventions over two years revealed that the current budget was sufficient to scale up HTS as part of a broader package of social-behavioral change efforts and for infants born to mothers with HIV. However, additional HTS for the general population was deemed unaffordable. Cost per person diagnosed as HIV-positive is a useful proxy indicator for cost-effectiveness. This metric can also include the cost per person diagnosed and linked to treatment, particularly in settings with high levels of retesting among individuals who already know their HIV status. The scale of HTS approaches is critical for achieving public health impact. While some HTS approaches may have a low cost per person diagnosed, they may only reach a small, focused group. Therefore, programs must also consider the absolute number of people diagnosed with HIV through different HTS approaches to assess their value in achieving national targets. HTS approaches with higher costs per person tested may still be valuable if they achieve a cost per person diagnosed (and linked to treatment) that is comparable to or lower than other approaches. For example, community-based outreach for key populations, HIVST, partner services, and provider-assisted referral can be resource-intensive but are essential for identifying infections among individuals who might not otherwise test. These approaches are also crucial for improving equity among underserved populations. Limited resources may necessitate a more focused implementation of cost-effective HTS approaches. To optimize resources, these approaches may need to target specific populations, such as key populations, individuals with indicator conditions or symptoms associated with HIV, or specific geographic settings or health facilities. Cost, cost-effectiveness, and budget impact analyses are vital components of a comprehensive situational analysis and broader decision-making processes to determine which HTS approaches to scale up and which to discontinue.
